title: Delirium and agitation
banner: DRAFT, NOT clinically reviewed. Fictional scenario specification; never imported, published or shown to learners.
learning_objectives: Recognise changes that may indicate delirium, including hypoactive delirium, and arrange an assessment with the critical-care tool.
Use verbal and non-verbal de-escalation and reorientation before any medicine is considered.
Recognise that diagnosis and medicines are for the responsible clinicians.

sources.use: NICE CG103 (updated January 2023): recommendations on recognising, preventing, assessing and initially managing delirium
FDA haloperidol label: QT and cardiovascular warnings

required_sources: Critical-care delirium guidance read in full (for example PADIS statements on prevention, sedation and mobilisation)
Licence terms and training requirements for CAM-ICU and ICDSC (not read)
Unit delirium and agitation protocol and medicine policy
gaps: No published clinical scenario may exist until the review phase: this is a specification only.
The branching content, consequences and scoring are the author's reading of the cited sources and have had no clinical review.
The tools are named only; their items and scoring are not reproduced and were not read.
Doses, routes and durations of any medicine are deliberately absent; NICE places medicine use after failed de-escalation and with prescriber and MHRA safety considerations.
NICE CG103 covers hospital and long-term care in the UK; critical-care-specific sedation and pain management were not read.
permissions: Cited sources are paraphrased only; see the licensing register for each source's reproduction status.
NICE: Notice of rights not read; paraphrase only.
setting: A fictional adult on a fictional critical care unit.

steps.info: A patient who was calm yesterday is now restless at night, pulling at tubing and not following simple requests. A colleague says the patient is just difficult.

options.text: Treat the recent change as possible delirium, make sure the patient is safe, carry out or request an assessment with the unit's critical-care delirium tool by someone competent, and report the findings to the team.
options.feedback: NICE says recent changes in cognition, behaviour or movement should prompt an assessment, and that in critical care CAM-ICU or ICDSC is used by a competent practitioner, with the final diagnosis made by a clinician with the right expertise.
options.consequence: The tool assessment is done and the responsible clinician is told.

options.text: Treat it as a personality issue and settle the patient with a sedative from the ward stock.
options.feedback: A recent change needs assessing, not labelling; medicines are prescribed, and NICE places them after de-escalation has failed.
options.consequence: The behaviour worsens and the cause is not looked for.

options.text: Wait until the next shift to see whether the patient settles.
options.feedback: NICE says to assess promptly once changes are noticed.

steps.info: The clinician has diagnosed delirium. The patient is distressed and frightened and tries to climb out of bed.

observations.label: Behaviour
observations.value: Distressed, trying to get out of bed

options.text: Stay with the patient, use calm verbal and non-verbal de-escalation, explain where they are, who they are and what your role is, involve family if possible, report ongoing distress or risk to the team, and give any medicine only if it has been prescribed.
options.feedback: NICE says to try verbal and non-verbal de-escalation first, give effective communication and reorientation, consider involving family, and only consider short-term medicine if de-escalation fails; the prescriber decides.
options.consequence: The patient calms a little and the team reviews the underlying causes.

options.text: Give haloperidol from stock as soon as the patient becomes distressed.
options.feedback: Medicines are prescribed after de-escalation has been tried, with attention to safety warnings such as QT effects.
options.consequence: The medicine is given without an order and without the checks the label warns about.

options.text: Leave the patient alone so that nothing provokes them.
options.feedback: Staying away leaves the patient frightened and at risk; NICE advises communication, reorientation and reassurance.
options.consequence: The patient's distress and risk increase.

steps.info: The patient is calmer. The team is looking for the cause of the delirium.
steps.prompt: What should you continue to do?

observations.label: Environment
observations.value: Clock and calendar not yet visible

observations.label: Care team
observations.value: Several different staff in recent shifts

options.text: Keep up the prevention measures: familiar staff where possible, clock and calendar in view, reorientation, hydration, mobility as the team allows, avoiding unnecessary catheters, and watch for quiet, withdrawn changes that suggest hypoactive delirium; document the diagnosis and the response.
options.feedback: NICE lists a tailored multicomponent package, vigilance for hypoactive delirium and documentation of the diagnosis.
options.consequence: The patient is better orientated and the record is complete for the next shift.

options.text: Stop reorientation because it is not a treatment.
options.feedback: NICE recommends communication and reorientation as part of managing delirium.

options.text: Move the patient to a quieter room away from the familiar team.
options.feedback: NICE advises avoiding moving people unless absolutely necessary and keeping a familiar team.
options.consequence: The move disorients the patient further.

learning_points: New confusion, restlessness or withdrawal can be delirium: assess with the critical-care tool and report.
De-escalate, reorientate and involve family before any medicine; medicines are prescribed.
Keep prevention measures going, watch for hypoactive delirium and document.
